entry: Subfamily of mostly evergreen perennial flowering plants in the grass family, Poaceae. It grows mainly in tropical and subtropical regions, especially in Asia, and is used as a building material, a food and a raw product, with economic and cultural significance in [[South Asia]], [[Southeast Asia]] and [[East Asia]]. Giant bamboos are the largest members of the grass family; *Dendrocalamus sinicus* has stalks (culms) reaching 46 m in length and 36 cm in diameter. Certain species grow 91 cm in 24 hours, and growth of up to 120 cm in 24 hours has been observed in Japanese giant timber bamboo (*Phyllostachys bambusoides*). Bamboo is a natural [[Composite material|composite material]] with a strength-to-weight ratio similar to timber. *Bambusa tulda* of [[Bangladesh]] and [[India]] has been tested at tensile strengths as high as 400 MPa (60,000 psi).

Elongated, edible fruit, botanically a [[Berry (botany)|berry]], produced by large treelike herbaceous plants of the genus *Musa*. Almost all modern seedless cultivated bananas come from two wild species, *Musa acuminata* and *Musa balbisiana*, or their hybrids. Musa species are native to tropical Indomalaya and Australia and were probably domesticated in [[New Guinea]]. Bananas are grown mainly for their fruit and, to a lesser extent, for banana paper and textiles. In 2022, [[India]] and [[China]] were the world's largest producers, together accounting for approximately 26% of total production. Panama disease, caused by a *Fusarium* [[Fungus|fungus]], and black sigatoka threaten the [[Cultivar|Cavendish]] bananas that are the main kind eaten in the Western world. Because commercial varieties are seedless, breeding new varieties is difficult, so banana germplasm is conserved in gene banks around the world.

National park and [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]] on the west coast of [[Mauritania]], between Nouakchott and Nouadhibou. Established in 1976 to protect its natural resources and fisheries, the park has extensive mudflats used by over two million migrant waders from northern [[Europe]], [[Siberia]] and [[Greenland]]. Between 25,000 and 40,000 pairs of 15 species nest there, making the largest colonies of water birds in [[West Africa]]; at least 108 bird species have been recorded. Flamingos, pelicans and terns breed on its sand banks, and orca, pilot whales and Mediterranean monk seals are among the marine mammals seen. About 500 Imraguen people live in seven villages within the park and fish using traditional methods, and no motor boats are permitted. Targeting of sharks and rays, which is not allowed, is described as perhaps the most challenging conservation issue in the park.

Material or medical device used to support a wound or injury, or to provide compression. Bandages used in healing protect the area from contamination and further trauma, and tight bandages can slow blood flow to a bleeding arm or leg. The most common type is the gauze, or roller, bandage, a woven strip available in many widths and lengths. Adhesive, liquid and triangular bandages are also used. A triangular bandage, also called a cravat bandage, is a right-angled piece of cloth that can serve as a sling or be folded for other uses; the [[Scouting|Scouting movement]] popularized it in first aid lessons. Compression bandages include short-stretch types, applied to treat lymphedema or venous ulcers and considered safe for long-term treatment, and long-stretch types, which have a very high resting pressure and must be removed at night. In 2016 a bandage inspired by kirigami, with parallel slits to fit bending areas of the body, was invented; it has been produced with 3D-printed molds.

Capital city of West Java province, [[Indonesia]]. Located on the western highland of [[Java]], Bandung lies in a river basin surrounded by volcanic mountains that provided a natural defense, a reason the [[Dutch East Indies]] government planned to move the capital from Batavia (modern-day Jakarta). The Dutch established tea plantations in the mountains in the 18th century, and in 1906 the Dutch population won a municipal government. The city became a resort for Europeans, and the shops selling fashion from Paris earned it the nickname Parijs van Java. After Indonesian independence in 1945 it urbanized rapidly, facing problems with waste, floods and traffic. The first Asian-African Conference, the Bandung Conference, was hosted there by President [[Sukarno]] in 1955. The city joined the [[UNESCO]] Creative Cities Network in 2015, and it is Indonesia's major technology centre.

Canada's first national park, in the Rocky Mountains of [[Alberta]]. Established in 1885 as Rocky Mountains Park, it covers 6,641 sq km of mountainous terrain 110–180 km west of [[Calgary]], with many [[Glacier|glaciers]], ice fields, dense coniferous forest and alpine landscapes. The Columbia Icefield is the largest uninterrupted glacial mass in the Rockies. Mammals include grizzly bear, cougar, wolverine, elk, bighorn sheep and moose. Before the park was established, the Stoney Nakoda and other [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous]] peoples hunted and travelled in the area. Construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway through the park began in 1875, and its hotels attracted tourists. Annual visits exceeded 4.5 million as of 2025. In the mid-1990s Parks Canada began a two-year study, which led to policies aimed at preserving ecological integrity.

Armed conflict from 25 March to 16 December 1971 between the Pakistani military and Bengali nationalist forces, which led to the independence of [[Bangladesh]]. It began with Operation Searchlight, a Pakistani army crackdown on Bengali intellectuals, students and military personnel in [[Dhaka]], which initiated the [[Genocide|genocide]]. The Mukti Bahini, a guerrilla force of Bengali defectors, paramilitary units and civilians, fought back. India joined the war on 3 December 1971, and Pakistan surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December, in what remains the largest surrender of armed personnel since the Second World War. An estimated 10 million Bengali refugees fled to India, and 30 million were internally displaced. Estimates of civilian deaths range from 300,000 to 3 million; Bangladesh's official figure is 3 million, while independent assessments often place the toll lower. The war was a major episode in [[Cold War]] tensions, and most UN member states recognized Bangladesh as a sovereign nation in 1972.

City (pop., 2020: 889,231), capital of the [[Central African Republic]]. It lies on the northern bank of the Ubangi River, near the border with the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. Established as a French outpost in 1889, it marked the limit of navigable water north from [[Brazzaville]]. Bangui is the administrative, trade and commercial centre of the country, home to the National Assembly, government buildings, banks, embassies and main markets. The city manufactures textiles, food products, [[Beer|beer]], shoes and soap. Its Notre-Dame Cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Bangui, and the University of Bangui was inaugurated in 1970. The city has been at the centre of the country's instability, including coups and rebellions since the 1960s.

Australian bush poet, journalist and author. Born in rural [[New South Wales]], Paterson worked as a lawyer, qualifying as a solicitor, before turning to literature. He wrote many of his best-known poems for the nationalist journal *The Bulletin*, including "Clancy of the Overflow" (1889) and "The Man from Snowy River" (1890). His 1895 ballad "Waltzing Matilda" is regarded as Australia's unofficial national anthem; according to the National Film and Sound Archive, it has been recorded more than any other Australian song. Paterson reported from the [[Second Boer War]], drove ambulances on the Western Front during World War I, and served as a remount officer in the Middle East. In 1939 he received the Commander of the Order of the British Empire for his literary contributions.

American multinational banking and financial services holding company, headquartered in [[Charlotte, North Carolina]]. It was formed in 1998, when NationsBank acquired BankAmerica for $62 billion and adopted the Bank of America name. Its history traces to the Bank of Italy, founded in San Francisco in 1904 by Amadeo Pietro Giannini to serve immigrants whom established banks excluded. It is the second-largest U.S. bank by consolidated assets, after [[JPMorgan Chase]], and its investment banking is headquartered in [[Manhattan]]. Its market share has led to numerous lawsuits and investigations concerning mortgages and disclosures dating back to the [[2008 financial crisis|2008 financial crisis]]. Regulatory fines have exceeded $80 billion since 2008.

Legal process by which people or other entities unable to repay creditors may obtain relief from some or all of their debts. In most jurisdictions it is imposed by court order, often initiated by the debtor. Bankruptcy is not a synonym for insolvency, since an insolvent person may hold other legal statuses. The process can involve asset liquidation, debt restructuring or negotiated repayment plans, providing for orderly distribution to creditors and rehabilitation of debtors. Formal statutes emerged in 16th-century England under Henry VIII. In the [[United States]], the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 provides chapter 7 for liquidation, chapter 11 for business reorganization and chapter 13 for individual repayment. U.S. cases rose to 517,308 in 2024, a 14.2% increase.

Pseudonymous England-based street artist, political activist and film director. His identity has never been publicly confirmed. His satirical stencil graffiti on walls and bridges around the world comments on war, consumerism and institutional power, and his work grew out of the [[Bristol]] underground scene. He directed the documentary *Exit Through the Gift Shop* (2010), which was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. The work *Girl with Balloon* sold for £1.04 million at Sotheby's in 2018, after which a concealed shredder partially destroyed it; the altered piece, retitled *Love Is in the Bin*, later fetched £18.6 million.

Female spirit in [[Ireland|Irish]] folklore who heralds the death of a family member by screaming, wailing or keening. Her name, from Irish *bean sí*, means "woman of the fairy mound" or "fairy woman", and it connects her to the *síde*, or mounds, of the Irish countryside. She is often attached to ancient Gaelic families and may appear as an elderly hag, a youthful woman in white or gray, or a washerwoman scrubbing bloodied clothes. Her cry is most often heard at night near the home of the soon-to-die. Scholars describe her as a sorrowful messenger rather than a malevolent entity.

Series of prehistoric migrations of Proto-Bantu-speaking peoples from an original nucleus in West-Central Africa across [[Central Africa]], Eastern Africa and [[Southern Africa]]. The settlers absorbed, displaced and in some cases replaced the hunter-gatherer and pastoralist groups they met, and genetic evidence indicates admixture with local populations. Linguistic evidence supports the expansion; the linguistic core of the [[Bantu languages]] lies from north-western [[Cameroon]] to southern [[Nigeria]]. The expansion is believed to have taken place between about 6,000 and 1,500 years ago (approximately 4,000 BC to 500 AD). One branch reached central Angola around 500 BC, while the Eastern Stream reached west of [[Lake Victoria]] around 500 BC. The expansion spread farming, iron technology and pottery, and reached South Africa, probably as early as 300 AD.

Language family, or branch of the proposed Niger-Congo family, spoken across Central, Southern, Eastern and Southeast Africa by the [[Bantu peoples]]. The total number of distinct Bantu languages is estimated at between 440 and 680, depending on whether a variety is classed as a language or a dialect, and many borrow words from one another. About 350 million people spoke them in 2015, roughly 30% of Africa's population. About one-sixth of speakers, and one-third of the languages, are found in the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. Swahili is the most widely spoken, with 16 million native speakers and 80 million second-language speakers (2015), and is a lingua franca of the East African Community. Many Bantu languages are tonal and share a noun class system in which prefixes mark singular and plural forms.

Ethnolinguistic grouping of approximately 400 distinct Indigenous African ethnic groups who speak [[Bantu languages|Bantu languages]]. They inhabit a vast area from West Africa to Central, Eastern and Southern Africa. In the mid-2010s, about 350 million speakers, roughly 30% of Africa's population, spoke these languages. The [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]] alone has about 90 million speakers (2015), divided into some 400 ethnic or tribal groups. The larger groups include the Zulu of [[South Africa]] (14.2 million as of 2016) and the Shona of Zimbabwe (17.6 million as of 2020). Their ancestors spread through the [[Bantu expansion|Bantu expansion]]. Interpretations of the migrations differ: some describe peaceful diffusion, others conquest and subjugation, while recent archaeogenetic studies report demographic replacement tempered by gene flow.

Christian rite of initiation, almost invariably involving water. It may be performed by sprinkling or pouring water on the head, or by partial or complete immersion, traditionally three times, once for each person of the Trinity. Baptism is regarded as a sacrament in most churches and an ordinance in others. In the [[Catholic Church]], [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Eastern Orthodox Church]] and Lutheran churches it is the door to church membership. Catholic and Lutheran theology regard it as necessary for salvation, though not without exception, while [[Huldrych Zwingli]] denied its necessity. Quakers, some Unitarians and the Salvation Army do not practice water baptism. The majority of Christians baptize infants, while [[Baptists]] regard only believer's baptism as true baptism. Mandaeans undergo repeated baptism for purification rather than initiation.

Protestant tradition of Christianity that baptizes only believers, by total immersion. Modern Baptist churches generally hold the priesthood of all believers, sola scriptura and congregationalist polity, in which each local congregation governs itself. Baptists recognize two ordinances, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Baptists trace their origins to Dissenters from the [[Church of England]]; a congregation formed in [[Amsterdam]] rejected infant baptism, and Thomas Helwys returned the congregation to [[England]], where he argued for the separation of church and state. English Baptists divided into General Baptists, who held that Christ's atonement extended to all people, and Particular Baptists, who held that it extended only to the elect. The Baptist World Alliance unites 253 bodies in 130 countries. In 1845 the Southern Baptist Convention was formed after a split over whether slaveholders could serve as missionaries.

Retail business that serves alcoholic beverages for consumption on its premises. Also called a saloon, tavern, tippling house, pub or club, a bar typically sells beer, wine, liquor, [[Cocktail|cocktails]] and soft drinks, often with snacks. The term derives from the metal or wooden bar, or barrier, along a countertop where drinks are served; the counters are 18–24 inches (0.46–0.61 m) deep. Bars evolved into structured establishments by the 17th century in Europe and colonial America. In the United States, they emerged from taverns that also offered lodging and meals, and adapted after Prohibition (1920–1933). Bars operate under regulations on age, operating hours and capacity, and studies have found that later closing times correlate with higher assault densities near venues.

Metric unit of pressure equal to 100,000 pascals (Pa). It is not part of the [[International System of Units]] (SI), though the SI brochure lists it, and it has been legally recognized in the [[European Union]] since 2004. One bar is slightly less than average atmospheric pressure at sea level, which is about 1.013 bar. The bar and the millibar were introduced by the Norwegian meteorologist Vilhelm Bjerknes. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology deprecates its use except for limited use in meteorology.

44th president of the United States, from 2009 to 2017. A member of the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], he was the first African American to hold the office. He represented Illinois in the U.S. Senate from 2005 to 2008. He was awarded the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts in international diplomacy, a decision that drew both praise and criticism. His administration responded to the [[2008 financial crisis|2008 financial crisis]] with the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 and the Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, and it oversaw the implementation of the Affordable Care Act. The raid that killed Osama bin Laden, leader of [[Al-Qaeda]], was ordered during his presidency, and the number of American soldiers in [[Afghanistan]] decreased during his second term. He negotiated the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action with Iran and normalized relations with Cuba. He was the first sitting U.S. president to publicly support same-sex marriage.

Island nation in the [[Lesser Antilles]] of the West Indies, in the [[Atlantic Ocean]] (pop., 2024: 304,139). It is the southernmost and easternmost island of the [[Caribbean]] region, and its capital and largest city is Bridgetown. Spanish navigators claimed the island in the late 15th century, and English settlers arrived in 1627, after which it became an English and later British colony with a plantation economy. Slavery continued until it was phased out through most of the [[British Empire]] by the Slavery Abolition Act 1833; the descendants of enslaved Africans now account for over 90% of the population. Barbados became independent on 30 November 1966 as a monarchy within the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], with [[Elizabeth II]] as queen. On 30 November 2021 it became a parliamentary republic. Tourism and international financial services drive its economy, which has diversified from sugar production.

American actress and singer, known for the title role in the [[NBC]] sitcom *I Dream of Jeannie* (1965–1970). Her other films include *Flaming Star* (1960), opposite [[Elvis Presley]], and *Harper Valley P.T.A.* (1978). After *I Dream of Jeannie* she appeared mostly in dramatic roles, and she later appeared in five episodes of the final season of [[Dallas (TV series)|Dallas]]. Her memoirs are *Barbara Eden: My Story* (1986) and *Jeannie Out of the Bottle* (2011).

American novelist, essayist and poet. Her widely known works include *The Poisonwood Bible*, about a missionary family in the Congo, and *Animal, Vegetable, Miracle*, a nonfiction account of her family's attempts to eat locally. She won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2023 for *Demon Copperhead*. Her work often focuses on social justice, [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]] and the relationship between humans and their environments. She was raised in rural [[Kentucky]] and lives in [[Appalachia|Appalachia]], and in 2000 she established the Bellwether Prize to support "literature of social change."

American cytogeneticist and Nobel laureate whose research on [[Maize|maize]] chromosomes led to the discovery of transposons. She received her PhD in botany from [[Cornell University]] in 1927 and developed techniques for visualizing maize chromosomes. Her microscopic analysis demonstrated genetic recombination by crossing-over during meiosis, and she showed the role of the telomere and centromere in conserving genetic information. During the 1940s and 1950s she discovered transposons and showed that genes control the expression of physical characteristics. Because of skepticism toward her work, she stopped publishing her data in 1953. Her findings were confirmed in the 1960s and 1970s. She received the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine in 1983 for the discovery of genetic transposition; as of 2025 she remains the only woman to have received an unshared Nobel Prize in that category.
